We bet that build speed, not the feature list, was the moat.
I grew the platform line from $18M to $63M ARR through seven product leads.
The trade-off was build speed for every team against custom work for the largest accounts.
We decided to stop the plugin marketplace so the org could focus on build time.
The platform became a line of business with its own revenue target.
Developers who wait on builds churn, so speed mattered more than new integrations.
I chose to enter the enterprise segment because it built on our existing strength in caching.
The investment case was simple: owning scheduling protects the core business.
Margins improved because we priced build minutes per team instead of per seat.
Our market was mid-size engineering teams that the big clouds underserved.
Through the directors, the org cut median build time 44% in 15 months.
I said no to three partner integrations that would have diluted the platform bet.
Why this team: you are hiring to fix the same problem I solved at a smaller scale.
Retention, not acquisition, was the constraint on growth.
We killed the desktop client to put every engineer on the teams who pay for build minutes.
The board wanted more logos; I argued the real goal was profitable expansion.
Our moat was the build data from 41,000 teams that no competitor could buy.
I set the strategy and let the product leads own the decisions in their areas.
The core business was hosted CI; everything else had to feed it.
We priced the new tier at cost to serve plus a reliability premium.
We built a build cache with a drag-and-drop config editor.
I set up a weekly reliability review meeting with the on-call leads.
We moved release checks into a single workflow tool.
The team shipped a new dashboard for flaky tests.
I wrote the PRD and the specs for the runner autoscaling flow.
We ran A/B tests on the onboarding email copy.
We migrated the test sharding logic to a new pipeline.
I instrumented the setup funnel with event tracking.
We automated the dependency upgrade step with a bot.
Our sprint cadence moved from two weeks to one.
I configured the alert thresholds in the monitoring tool.
We added a button to rerun only the failed jobs.
The API returns cache hits in under 50 milliseconds.
I used Claude Code and Cursor to prototype the build log viewer.
I joined Quillstone in 2021.
Before that I spent four years at Tidewell Software.
Thank you for the time today.
I live in Chicago and can be in the office three days a week.
My background is in consulting and then product.
I studied economics and computer science.
